To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) 2-year-olds imitate selectively when they have the opportunity to do so and (b) 2-year-old children are more likely to imitatively faithful after playing a mimicry task with a peer than after an instrumental game with the same peer.

(a) children are more likely to imitatively faithfully (i.e., overimitate) when the demonstrator is a peer than when the demonstrator does not have the same social status (e.g., an adult) and (b) this effect is present in 2-year-olds but not in 4-year-olds.

2-year-old children imitate selectively after playing with a person who performs a goal-directed action to obtain an object, whereas 4-year-old children imitated faithfully regardless of the prior game they played with the person.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether children's social context effects in 1 situation (i.e., selective imitation) are related to their social context effects in another situation (i.e. faithful imitation).
how children learn about social and physical causality and how they learn to use this knowledge in social contexts.
the development of social-cognitive skills in early childhood, and the role of social context in the development of these skills.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children imitate faithfully in a variety of social contexts, and selectively in others, but the social context in which children are placed has a greater effect on 2-year-olds than 4-year-olds.
4-year-olds are able to imitate selectively and faithfully, whereas 2-year-olds are more likely to imitated faithfully after a mimic game and to imitated selectively after an instrumental one.
children's social context effects in 3-year-olds are a function of the social-cognitive inductive inferences they make about the intentions and goals of their social partners.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social context effects in 1- to 4-year-olds’ imitation depend on both the age of the child and the social context.
2-year-olds are sensitive to the social context of the demonstration, and that this is reflected in their tendency to selectively versus faithfully imitate.
social context effects in imitation are not due to social priming, but to children's inferences about the social context, and that these inferences are more sophisticated in older children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children's tendency to faithfully imitate causally unnecessary actions is sensitive to their prior interactions with a model.

the social context in which children are asked to imitate has important consequences for their imitation behavior, and that the age at which children begin to overimitate may depend on the social context in question.
children's tendency to overimitate causally irrelevant actions is sensitive to social context effects and may not be an innate feature of human cognition.
